summary: Burning Activity Atlas is a web application for exploring NASA satellite-observed fire activity and comparing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot records. Users can view global monthly thermal-anomaly imagery on an interactive map or 3D globe, select a month, draw an area of interest, and generate a historical activity calendar. The analysis keeps raw detections and coverage for MODIS, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 distinct, while presenting active days, fire radiative power, and sensor-specific anomalies. An optional experimental bridge tests whether historical MODIS values can be expressed on a VIIRS reference scale; it is shown only when local validation improves on a baseline. The project helps users explore fire-season patterns and unusual periods while making data sources, coverage gaps, and uncertainty visible—without treating satellite hotspots as verified fires.
details:
Burning Activity Atlas is an independent web application for exploring historical satellite-detected burning activity. It presents monthly NASA GIBS thermal-anomaly imagery on a zoomable map and a 3D globe, with controls for browsing the archive. Users can select an area and calendar month to study observations across available years.

The project uses NASA FIRMS active-fire records and keeps MODIS and VIIRS platform data distinct, including product coverage and raw observations. Its comparison method places detections on a shared 1 km equal-area grid and counts unique cell-days. An optional MODIS-to-VIIRS overlap bridge is labeled experimental and shown only when its local validation performs better than a simple baseline.

The application is designed to help researchers, land managers, and emergency responders examine historical patterns and unusual periods. It does not identify confirmed fires, map fire perimeters, estimate burned area, issue operational warnings, or forecast fire spread. We built it as a JavaScript application on Cloudflare Workers, using MapLibre GL JS for mapping and NASA FIRMS and GIBS for fire records and imagery. The project’s main innovation is making sensor differences, coverage gaps, and uncertainty visible during exploration.
